Chapter 1 · From memory

Say the rule card back to me.

No notes. Before anything new, the class says last class's rule card back, word for word: “Permission first. Proof always.” Then three photographs go up side by side — one that travelled by mail, one from a real camera, one sitting in a portal — and the class says, from memory, what was missing in each.

Proof got faster, stricter, and easier to check over the years. That is the whole reason photo rules exist — and today those two little sentences run an entire work order.

Say her name first

She was named once, in Class 1, and she is never named again. If this is a new group, or the name needs saying out loud to bring her back — here it is. Pick the name the class chose, or type it in.

That's her — the 1972 house. Same house, fifth chapter.
Say it in class

“Permission first. Proof always. Last time, proof travelled by mail. Then by camera. Now it lives in a portal. The rule never changed. Permission first. Proof always.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

The rule card is the course in four words. Permission first: before anyone touches a house, someone has to have the right to be there. Proof always: whatever you do, you show it — with photographs and a report someone else can check. Everything in today's class is those four words, stretched across eleven stops. If a trainee remembers nothing else from the whole programme, these four words will still keep them out of the worst trouble this job has.

How to run the recall, step by step

  1. Ask for the rule card cold — no notes, no prompting, take the silence if it comes.
  2. If only half comes back, ask which half protects the family (“permission”) and which half protects the worker (“proof”).
  3. Then put the three photographs up: one mailed, one from a camera, one in a portal. Ask what was missing in each — the class answered this last time; make them answer it again from memory.
  4. Close in five minutes. Today is a journey, and the journey needs the whole hour.

If you've done this work before

You live inside this rule already, whether or not anyone ever wrote it on a card. Every held order, every re-shot photo, every “we can't bill that, there's no proof” — that's the card, working. Today makes the invisible visible for the people who are about to join you: they watch one order travel, and the card stops being a slogan and becomes the reason each stop exists.

The line to remember: “Permission first. Proof always.”

Where this comes from

The rule card and the three photographs are carried over from the class before this one, where proof's journey — mail, camera, portal — was taught in full. This class leans on that lesson rather than re-teaching it: the recall at the open is the check that it landed.

If this is all new to you

Once, proof was a photograph posted in an envelope and judged days later, by someone who never saw the house. Then cameras put dates on the film and the office could check a little more. Now proof lives in a portal — the client's own computer system, where work is sent and checked online — and it can be examined the same hour it was taken, against the order, line by line. Each era could check more than the one before. That's not a technology story; it's why the photo rules you'll learn later are as strict as they are.

How the checking changed, step by step

  1. By mail: slow, and the checker had to trust the envelope. What was missing: any way to verify when, or sometimes even where.
  2. By camera: faster, dates on frames — but still easy to stage, reuse, or send late.
  3. In a portal: uploaded against a specific order, visible to the client, comparable with the last visit. What can still be missing: the step nobody photographed.

If you've done this work before

Every processor knows the real gap in modern proof: it isn't blur, it's the missing middle — before and after with no during. Name that when the class answers, because it sets up this class's QC stop perfectly: the second pair of eyes exists to catch exactly the shot that isn't there.

The line to remember: “Proof got faster, stricter, and more checkable — the rule never changed.”

Where this comes from

The three-photo comparison is the closing image of the previous class, reused here as this class's opener — the programme teaches it once, then makes the class carry it. Nothing in this drawer adds new claims about the history; it's the same three artefacts, recalled.

Chapter 2 · The main character arrives

One morning, a letter arrives at the office. It isn't a letter.

It's a work order — a written instruction from a client. It says which house, what job, by when, and under which rulebook. That order is the main character of this class, and everything from here to the end of the course hangs on the journey it's about to take.

Eleven stops. Many hands. One instruction, travelling. Follow the order, and you understand the whole business.

Say it in class

“A work order is a written instruction from a client: which house, what job, by when, and under which rulebook. That order is the main character today.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

Read any work order and you'll find the same four things, however it's formatted. Which house — the address everything attaches to. What job — the work being asked for, in the client's words. By when — the deadline the whole chain organises itself around. Under which rulebook — the set of rules that governs this job: what counts as done, what proof is needed, what it pays. Trainees who learn to find those four things on any order, from any client, can walk into any office in this industry and start reading.

How to read one, step by step

  1. Find the address first. Everything else belongs to that house.
  2. Find the job, in the client's own words — not your guess at the words.
  3. Find the deadline, and count backwards from it: field day, QC day, submission day.
  4. Find the rulebook named on the order. That one — not the one you used yesterday for a different client.

If you've done this work before

The failure mode you already know: an order read for three of its four things. The deadline everyone saw; the rulebook nobody checked — and the proof comes back shot to the wrong client's standard, unbillable. When you teach this slide, say the quiet part: the fourth thing is the one that pays you, and it's the one most often skipped.

The line to remember: “Which house, what job, by when, under which rulebook.”

Where this comes from

This four-part reading of a work order is the programme's own definition, taught identically in every class from here on — it's the vocabulary the later sessions (the work itself, then money) all assume. The order in today's story is a teaching example, not a real client's order.

If this is all new to you

Every client writes its own rules: how a lawn must look before it's billable, which photos prove a lock was changed, how many days you get. So the same job — cut a lawn — can be three slightly different jobs for three different clients. The rule that keeps you safe sounds almost too simple: the governing rulebook is the one written on the order in your hand. Never another client's rules. Never what you remember from last time. The order in your hand.

How mistakes happen here, step by step

  1. A crew does a job well — by the standards of the client they worked for yesterday.
  2. The proof goes in, shot and finished to the wrong rulebook.
  3. The client checks against their rules — the ones on the order — and the work fails review.
  4. The job was done. The order still wasn't. That's the difference this slide exists to teach.

If you've done this work before

Put a name on it for the class: rulebook bleed — one client's habits leaking into another client's job. It is the most expensive beginner mistake in a multi-client office, precisely because the work itself looks fine. The defence is boring and total: read the rulebook off the order, every order, every time, out loud if you have to.

The line to remember: “Never another client's rules. Never last time's memory. The order in your hand.”

Where this comes from

No numbers hide in this drawer — it's a working rule of the programme, stated the same way in the course materials and on the wall map the class builds next. Later classes teach individual clients' rulebooks one at a time; this class teaches only how to tell them apart.

Chapter 3 · The wall map

Eleven stops, in order. Every later class hangs on this map.

Here is the whole journey on one wall: order → intake → permission gate → dispatch → field → proof → QC → invoice → submission → payment → follow-up. One work order travels through many hands, and every hand has the same job: pass it on clean — or stop it honestly.

Learn this map once, properly, and every class after this one is just a closer look at a stop you already know.

1 · OrderThe instruction arrives
→
2 · IntakeRead it properly
→
3 · Permission gateDo we have the right?
→
4 · DispatchThe right crew
→
5 · FieldThe work, at the house
→
6 · ProofPhotos and report
→
7 · QCA second pair of eyes
→
8 · InvoiceThe bill, from proven work
→
9 · SubmissionInto the client's system
→
10 · PaymentAfter the client's review
→
11 · Follow-upUntil it's all accounted for
Say it in class

“One order, eleven stops, many hands. Your job at every stop is the same: pass it on clean, or stop it honestly.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

Walk it slowly once. The order arrives. At intake, someone reads it properly before anyone moves. At the permission gate, the office asks whether it has the right to touch this house at all. Dispatch sends the right crew. In the field, the crew does the work and photographs it as they go. That photography is the proof. QC — quality check — is a second pair of eyes on the proof. The invoice bills only what was approved and proven. Submission sends the finished file into the client's system. Payment comes after the client's review. And follow-up tracks the order until every dollar and every answer is accounted for. Eleven stops — that's the whole map.

How to put it on the wall, step by step

  1. Say the eleven names once, slowly, pointing at each card as you go.
  2. Say them again, faster — the class joining in by the gate.
  3. Then walk it backwards from payment: “Before payment?” — “Submission.” “Before submission?” — “Invoice.” Backwards is how faults get traced in real life, so teach it both ways now.
  4. Leave the map up for the rest of the course. Every later session points at it.

If you've done this work before

Notice what's not a stop: “the work” is one stop of eleven. Beginners think the field is the job. This map is the correction — the field is where the job becomes visible, but the job is won or lost at intake, at the gate, at QC, and in follow-up, by people the client never sees. If you supervise others, this map is also your diagnostic: when an order goes wrong, the first question is never “who messed up,” it's “at which stop?”

The line to remember: “Pass it on clean, or stop it honestly.”

Where this comes from

The eleven-stop lifecycle is the programme's own spine — the same sequence the course's later sessions each take one piece of: the work sessions live at stops 5–6, the money session at stops 8–11. It is a teaching map of how an order moves through an office like this one, not a claim about any one company's internal system.

If this is all new to you

The order of the stops isn't tidiness — it's dependency. You can't dispatch before intake, because nobody yet knows what's actually being asked. You can't pass the gate after the crew is already at the house — the right to enter has to be settled before anyone travels. You can't invoice before QC, because the bill is built from proof that survived checking. Shuffle the stops and each one loses the thing it needs from the one before. That's why the map is taught as a sequence, not a pile.

How a shuffle hurts, step by step

  1. Dispatch before intake: a crew drives out with yesterday's understanding of the job.
  2. Field before the gate: work starts on a house nobody has confirmed the right to enter.
  3. Invoice before QC: the bill goes out carrying a gap QC would have caught — and the client finds it instead.
  4. Each shuffle moves the discovery of the mistake one stop closer to the client. The map exists to discover mistakes at home.

If you've done this work before

Here's the version worth saying to experienced hires: the stops are also where the money changes state. Before the gate, the order is information. After the field, it's cost — fuel, hours, materials already spent. After submission, it's a claim. After payment, it's revenue. A stop skipped early is cheap; the same fault found late has already been paid for once. That's the economics under the map, and it's why “we'll catch it at QC” is never a plan for a gate question.

The line to remember: “Discover mistakes at home, not at the client's desk.”

Where this comes from

The dependencies named here are drawn straight from the stop definitions themselves — each stop's description in the course materials names what it receives from the stop before. No outside source is needed, and none is claimed.

Chapter 4 · Stop 2

Intake: read the whole order, slowly, before anyone moves.

Intake is the first real stop, and the quietest — and it may be the most important one on the wall. Someone in the office reads the whole order, slowly, and writes down what is actually asked: the scope — the exact work covered, and nothing more — and the rulebook that governs it.

An order skimmed in a hurry becomes a crew sent to the wrong job. An order read properly becomes a job done right.

Say it in class

“Intake is where most mistakes are born — or prevented. Read the whole order, slowly, and write down what is actually asked.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

The scope is the border of the job. If the order says cut the lawn and change the front lock, then the lawn and the front lock are the job — not the back lock, not the hedge, not the broken window you happened to notice. Work outside the scope isn't generosity; it's unpaid, unapproved, and sometimes unauthorised. Work missing from inside the scope is the opposite failure: the order asked, and nobody did it. Intake is where the border gets drawn clearly enough that both failures become rare.

How intake is done, step by step

  1. Read the whole order once, without writing anything. Get the shape of it.
  2. Read it again with a pen. Write the scope as a plain list — one line per task, in your own words.
  3. Write the rulebook's name beside the list, from the order itself.
  4. Note the deadline, the address, and anything the order flags — access notes, hazards, special instructions.
  5. Anything unclear gets a question now, at the desk — not a guess later, at the house.

If you've done this work before

The intake habit that separates senior processors: they write the scope for the crew, not for themselves. A scope note that only makes sense to its writer fails at dispatch. Test yours by the stranger standard — could a crew member who has never seen this order do the right job from your note alone? If not, the intake isn't finished, however carefully the order was read.

The line to remember: “The scope is the exact work covered — and nothing more.”

Where this comes from

Intake and scope are defined this way in the course materials, and every later session uses the words exactly like this. No figures are involved — this stop is a reading discipline, not a statistic.

If this is all new to you

Think about where a mistake costs least. A wrong address caught at intake costs a corrected note. The same wrong address caught in the field costs a wasted drive. Caught at submission, it costs a rejected file. Caught by the client, it costs trust. Nothing about the mistake changed — only the stop where it was found. Intake is the stop where every mistake is still cheap, which is why this quiet desk work, done slowly, protects everyone downstream.

How an intake mistake travels, step by step

  1. The order is skimmed; one line of the scope is missed.
  2. Dispatch sends a crew briefed on the skimmed version.
  3. The field does exactly what it was told — the missed line, not done.
  4. Proof can't show work that never happened; QC flags a gap, or worse, doesn't.
  5. The order bounces back days later, at rush speed, at the worst possible price. One skipped line, five stops of cost.

If you've done this work before

You've lived the bounce-back. Use your own version of it when you teach this slide — a real pattern, no real addresses. The class should leave believing that slowness at intake is not the opposite of speed; it's where speed comes from. A crew that never has to go back is the fastest crew in the company.

The line to remember: “A mistake found at intake costs a note. Found at the client, it costs trust.”

Where this comes from

This is the course's own reasoning, stated in its materials and repeated on the wall map: intake is “where most mistakes are born or prevented.” It is a claim about this workflow, taught as such — not a measured statistic about the industry.

Chapter 5 · Stop 3

The gate asks one question, and only one: do we have the right?

A gate is a door you must pass before you are allowed to touch anything. The permission gate asks: do we have the right to enter this house and do this work? To answer it, you need one hard word — occupancy: whether someone still lives in the house.

A house can look empty and still be lived in. A family can be behind on payments and still be home. A house can be silent for a week and still belong to someone who sleeps there tonight.

Say it in class

“The gate is not paperwork. The gate is the question: do we have the right to be here? If the answer is not clear, we do not start.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

Occupancy sounds like a form word, but it means something human: is this still somebody's home? A house behind on its payments is not an empty house. A house with curtains drawn and a quiet street is not an empty house. Families travel, work nights, stay with relatives, come back. The gate's job is to slow the whole machine down at exactly this point and ask whether the right to enter has actually been established — not assumed, not hoped. Established.

How the gate is worked, step by step

  1. The order's occupancy information is read at intake and checked at the gate — two separate looks, on purpose.
  2. Whatever evidence exists is weighed: what the client states, what the record shows, what the last visit found.
  3. If the evidence says vacant and the right is clear, the order passes the gate.
  4. If anything contradicts, conflicts, or simply isn't there — the answer is not “probably fine.” The answer is the next slide.

If you've done this work before

The pressure at this stop is real and worth naming in front of trainees: deadlines pull one way, the gate pulls the other, and the gate feels like the obstacle. Reframe it early: the gate is not between the crew and the work — it's between the company and the one mistake that can't be undone with a re-visit. You can re-cut a lawn. You cannot un-enter a home.

The line to remember: “Empty-looking is not empty. Behind on payments is not the same as gone.”

Where this comes from

Occupancy is defined in the course materials as “whether someone still lives in the house,” and the gate's single question is quoted from them. The specifics of how occupancy gets verified for a given client live in that client's rulebook — this class teaches the gate, not any one client's checklist.

If this is all new to you

Changing a lock looks like the smallest job on any order — a few minutes, one tool. But think about what a lock does: it decides who may come home. The courtroom lesson from earlier in this course makes it plain: under the law in Washington, changing someone's lock can count as taking possession of their home — as saying, in effect, this house is no longer yours. A lock change done without the right is not a small error. It is the company declaring a family out of its own home. That is why the rule is authority first, work second — you check the right before you turn the key.

How the lesson connects, step by step

  1. A lock controls access to a home — that is its whole purpose.
  2. Changing it changes who holds that control.
  3. So the law can treat an unauthorised lock change as taking possession, not as a repair.
  4. Therefore the gate comes before the field, always — the right is checked while checking is still free.

If you've done this work before

Teach this without drama and without softening it. Trainees who understand why the gate exists stop experiencing it as bureaucracy. And be precise about the limit of the claim: the course teaches the Washington lesson as the illustration. Other states write their own rules — which is one more reason the rulebook on the order, and the office's authority check, govern each job rather than a trainee's memory of a classroom example.

The line to remember: “Authority first, work second. You check the right before you turn the key.”

An honest note on this one

The lock-and-possession point is taught the way the course materials teach it — as the Washington courtroom lesson carried over from earlier in the programme. It is presented here as a teaching illustration of why authority comes first, not as legal advice and not as a claim about every state's law. When a real order turns on a legal question, that question goes to the client's rulebook and up the chain — never to a classroom memory.

Chapter 6 · Stop 3, continued

If the right is not clear, you do not work. You stop.

The rule for an unclear answer has no exceptions: occupancy uncertain means HOLD and escalate. HOLD means do not start the work. Escalate means pass it upward, at once, to someone who can check properly.

HOLD is not a delay, and it is not laziness. HOLD is a decision — maybe the bravest one in this whole job.

Say it in class

“You will hold many orders in this job. Hold them well. That is the whole skill.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

The two words do different jobs. Hold stops the machine: no crew travels, no lock turns, no work begins on that order. Escalate starts a different machine: the question goes up, at once, to someone with the tools and authority to check occupancy properly. A hold without an escalation is just a stopped order gathering dust. An escalation without a hold is a question asked while the crew is already driving. The decision is the pair — always both, always together.

How a good hold happens, step by step

  1. The uncertainty is named, specifically — not “seems off,” but what was seen and what it might mean.
  2. The order is marked HOLD, so nobody downstream dispatches it by habit.
  3. The question goes up at once, with the specific uncertainty attached.
  4. The order waits — visibly, on the board, not buried — until the check comes back.
  5. When it clears, it re-enters the map at the gate, not halfway down it.

If you've done this work before

Notice how the hold protects twice. It protects the family that might still be home — the harm the gate exists to prevent. And it protects the company, and the crew member personally, from doing something they had no right to do. When you praise holds in front of a class — and you should, by name, whenever a trainee calls one — you are teaching them that this company would rather lose a day than take a home. That reputation is worth more than any deadline.

The line to remember: “Occupancy uncertain means HOLD and escalate. No exceptions.”

Where this comes from

The hold-and-escalate rule and its two definitions are quoted from the course materials, where they're stated without exception. The five-step handling above is the same rule unfolded into office practice, consistent with how the programme teaches the gate across its sessions.

If this is all new to you

Picture the moment. The order is due. The crew is ready. The house looks empty. Every pressure in the building says go — and one person says stop, because something small doesn't add up. That person will never be able to prove what they prevented. If they were right, a family kept its home one more lawful day and nobody ever knows. If they were wrong, a lawn got cut a day late. Hold those two outcomes side by side and the “brave” stops sounding dramatic — it's just the only weighing that makes sense.

How the two errors compare, step by step

  1. Wrongly held: the check runs, the house was empty, work happens a day or two later. Cost: a delay, explainable in one sentence.
  2. Wrongly approved: locks changed on a home someone still lives in. Cost: a family locked out, the law involved, the client relationship damaged — and no re-visit can undo the night it happened.
  3. The errors are not symmetrical, so the decision isn't either. Uncertainty breaks toward the hold, every time.

If you've done this work before

This asymmetry is the whole philosophy of the gate, and it's worth teaching as arithmetic, not virtue. Trainees don't need to be saints; they need to see that one error costs a day and the other costs something that can't be repaid. People protect what they understand. Give them the two columns and they'll hold orders for the rest of their careers without being watched.

The line to remember: “A wrong hold costs a day. A wrong approval costs a family its home.”

Where this comes from

The course materials call HOLD “the bravest decision in this whole job” and give the two protections named in the first drawer. The two-column comparison is that same teaching, spelled out — it introduces no new facts, and the classroom case on Slide 11 is where the class practises it.

Chapter 7 · Stops 4–5

Dispatch sends the right crew. The field is where the order meets the house.

Dispatch means sending the right crew to the right house — the crew with the right skill, in the right area, free on the right day, carrying the scope, the lockbox details, and the deadline. Then the map finally leaves the office: the field is the house itself, the crew on the ground, doing the work and photographing it as they go.

Everything before this stop was preparation. Everything after it is evidence. This is the hinge of the whole journey.

Say it in class

“The right crew, the right house, the right day — carrying the scope, the lockbox details, and the deadline.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

Dispatch sounds like “send someone.” It is really three matches at once. Skill: the crew can actually do this scope — a grass crew is not a lock crew. Area: the crew works near this house, so the day is spent working, not driving. Day: the crew is free early enough that the deadline survives a rainy morning. And the crew doesn't travel empty-headed: they carry the scope from intake, so they know the exact job; the access details; and the deadline, so they know what “late” means for this order.

How a dispatch is built, step by step

  1. Take the scope from intake — not a summary of it, the scope itself.
  2. Match the skill first: who can do this work, properly?
  3. Match the area: of those, who is already near this house?
  4. Match the day: who can be there with time to spare before the deadline?
  5. Hand over the whole packet: scope, access details, deadline. Then the stop is done — the order is moving.

If you've done this work before

The dispatch failure you'll recognise instantly: the nearest crew sent to a job beyond their skill because they were near. The lawn gets cut beautifully around a lock nobody could change, and the order makes the trip twice. Skill before distance, always — a longer drive beats a second trip, every week of the year.

The line to remember: “Skill first, then the map, then the calendar.”

Where this comes from

Dispatch's definition — right crew, right skill, right area, right day, carrying the scope, the lockbox details, and the deadline — is the course's own, from the lifecycle materials. Later sessions teach routing and crew planning in depth; this stop only has to be understood, and respected.

If this is all new to you

A lockbox is a small locked box that holds a house key, opened with a code. The crew gets the code from the order. Here's the discipline: the code must match the order exactly. If it doesn't work, the answer is never to guess, force, or improvise — a code that fails is information, and information travels back up the chain, the same way a hold does. Codes get changed, boxes get swapped, orders get transcribed wrong. All of those are office problems with office solutions, and none of them are solved at the door with a screwdriver.

How the field stop runs, step by step

  1. Arrive, and confirm you're at the order's house — address against order, before anything opens.
  2. Open the lockbox with the order's code. If it fails: stop, report, wait for instruction.
  3. Do the scope — the exact work, photographed as it happens (that's the next stop, and it starts here, not after).
  4. Leave the house secured the way the scope and rulebook require.
  5. The order moves to proof carrying everything the field saw — including anything unexpected, in the report, not in a phone call nobody recorded.

If you've done this work before

“Photographing it as they go” is the phrase to underline. Proof shot afterwards, from memory of what was done, is how during-photos go missing and QC gets its gaps. The field stop and the proof stop overlap on purpose: the camera is part of the work, not a chore after it. Crews who internalise that produce files QC waves through; crews who don't produce the re-visits everyone hates.

The line to remember: “The code matches the order exactly — and a code that fails is a message, not a puzzle.”

Where this comes from

The lockbox definition and the exact-match rule are quoted from the course materials. The field sequence follows from the lifecycle definitions of the field and proof stops; the detailed craft of each kind of field work is taught in the two classes after this one.

Chapter 8 · Stops 6–7

Proof shows what was done. QC asks whether the showing is enough.

Proof is the photos and the report that show what was done. QC — quality check — is a second pair of eyes that looks at the proof and asks: is every shot clear, is every step shown, is anything missing? If something is missing, the job goes back to the field. Gaps are never papered over.

The crew's eyes saw the house. QC's eyes see only the file — and the client will only ever see the file.

Say it in class

“Is every shot clear? Is every step shown? Is anything missing? If something is missing, the job goes back to the field. Gaps are never papered over.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

Nobody from the client's office will visit this house. Everything they will ever know about the work arrives as proof: the photographs and the written report. That makes proof a strange kind of stop — it isn't the work, but it's the only form in which the work survives. A job done perfectly and proven badly will be questioned, reduced, or refused. A job proven clearly tells its own story to a checker who wasn't there: what it looked like before, what was done, what it looks like now.

How good proof is built, step by step

  1. Photograph before the work starts — the house as found.
  2. Photograph during — the steps themselves, as the field stop produces them.
  3. Photograph after — the same views, finished.
  4. Write the report while the visit is fresh: what was done, what was found, anything the photos can't say.
  5. Send it up whole. The crew doesn't grade its own homework — that's the next stop.

If you've done this work before

The sentence trainees should hear from someone experienced: the client isn't buying your labour, they're buying your labour as proven. It sounds harsh until you've watched an unproven job get paid at zero. Teach proof as the product and the field work as its raw material, and the photo rules in the coming classes stop sounding like fussiness.

The line to remember: “The work ends at the house. The proof is what travels.”

Where this comes from

Proof's definition — “the photos and the report that show what was done” — is the course's. The before/during/after shape is how the programme's photo teaching is organised in the work sessions that follow; this class names the shape, those classes drill it house by house.

If this is all new to you

QC is not suspicion — it's a different chair. The crew knows what they did, so their eyes glide over the proof seeing the work. QC knows only what's in the file, so their eyes see the file the way the client will. Three questions do the whole job: is every shot clear? Is every step shown? Is anything missing? And the rule that gives those questions teeth: a gap sends the job back to the field. Nobody covers a gap with a hopeful sentence, a borrowed photo, or silence. Papered-over gaps are how small problems become fraud-shaped ones.

How a QC pass runs, step by step

  1. Read the scope first — QC checks proof against what was asked, not against what looks nice.
  2. Walk the proof in the order the work happened: before, during, after.
  3. Ask the three questions of every line of the scope.
  4. Pass it, and the order moves on — or name the exact gap and send it back to the exact stop that can fix it: the field.
  5. A sent-back job is information, not blame. The gap gets named so precisely that the re-visit fixes it in one trip.

If you've done this work before

Worth saying out loud in class: QC is the crew's protection, not their opponent. When a client's reviewer later challenges the file, a QC-passed file is the crew's alibi — every step shown, nothing resting on memory. The day a trainee gets saved by their own proof, they stop resenting this stop. Until then, they have to take it on trust — which is why this class makes the trust explicit.

The line to remember: “Is anything missing? Then it goes back. Gaps are never papered over.”

Where this comes from

QC's three questions and the goes-back rule are quoted from the course materials' lifecycle. The checking order above is those questions applied stop by stop — the programme's later sessions turn this stop into detailed checklists per work type.

Chapter 9 · Stops 8–9

The bill is built from proven work. Then it crosses into the client's world.

The invoice is the bill, built only from work that was approved and proven. Submission sends the finished file into the client's system. Keep this straight, because it matters for the whole course: the client's system is the client's portal — and it is never the same thing as the office engine, PPW, where the office prepares the work. Two systems. Never mixed.

Everything up to here happened in our house. Submission is the moment the order knocks on the client's door.

Say it in class

“The invoice is built only from work that was approved and proven. PPW is ours, where we prepare. The portal is theirs, where they receive. Two systems — never mixed.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

An invoice in this business isn't a wish list — it's a claim that specific work was authorised, done, and shown. So the bill is built backwards from the proof: this line exists because that work was in the scope, was done in the field, and survived QC. Work done outside the scope isn't on it. Work approved but unproven isn't on it. That discipline feels strict until you see the alternative: a bill padded with unprovable lines teaches the client to distrust every line, including the honest ones.

How an invoice is built, step by step

  1. Start from the QC-passed file — never from memory of the job.
  2. Take each line of the scope that was completed and proven.
  3. Price it by the rulebook on the order — the money session after next teaches the ladders in full.
  4. Every line must be able to point at its proof. If it can't point, it doesn't ship.

If you've done this work before

You know the word for what this stop prevents: leakage in both directions. Bill too little and the company quietly donates work; bill for the unproven and the company's name pays for it later, with interest, in the client's trust. “Approved and proven” is the whole ethics of invoicing in four words, and it's teachable in one slide because the stops before it did the work — scope defined it, the field did it, QC certified it.

The line to remember: “If a line can't point at its proof, it doesn't go on the bill.”

Where this comes from

The invoice's definition — “the bill, built only from work that was approved and proven” — is quoted from the course materials. Pricing itself is deliberately not taught here: rates, ladders, and client schedules belong to the money session, and nothing on this page invents a figure.

If this is all new to you

Two computer systems carry an order through its life, and they belong to different owners. The office engine — PPW — is our own system: where the office prepares the work, organises the proof, and builds the file. The client's portal is the client's system: where the client receives the finished file and checks it. Submission is the crossing between them. Say it as geography: work is prepared at home and delivered to the client's address. Nothing is “in the system” until you say which system.

How the crossing works, step by step

  1. The file is prepared and QC-passed inside the office engine.
  2. The invoice is built from that proven file.
  3. The finished file is submitted — sent into the client's portal.
  4. From that moment, the client's review begins, in their system, by their rulebook.
  5. Questions come back through the portal; answers and follow-up track them until they close — the last two stops.

If you've done this work before

Half the confused phone calls in this industry are two people using “the system” for different systems. Teach the class the reflex: name the system every time. “It's in PPW, not yet submitted” is a complete status. “It's in the system” is a riddle. Precision here is not pedantry — a file believed submitted while it sits in the office engine is a deadline quietly dying.

The line to remember: “PPW prepares. The portal receives. Never say ‘the system’ — say which one.”

Where this comes from

The two-systems distinction is stated in the course materials in exactly these terms — the office engine called PPW, the client's system called the portal, “two systems, never mixed” — and the whole course is built on keeping them apart. This page teaches the distinction; it shows no real screen, account, or client data from either system.

Chapter 10 · Stops 10–11

Submitted isn't finished. Paid and accounted for is finished.

Payment comes after the client's review — not when the work is done, not when the file is sent, but when the client has checked it and paid. And follow-up tracks the order until every dollar and every answer is accounted for. The journey is long, and that is the point.

An order nobody follows up doesn't end. It just goes quiet — and quiet orders are where money goes to be forgotten.

Say it in class

“Follow-up tracks the order until every dollar and every answer is accounted for. The journey is long — and that is the point.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

Beginners imagine the story ends at submission. In truth the client now does their version of everything you did: they read the file against the order, check the proof against their rulebook, and approve, reduce, or question the invoice. Only after that review does payment come. That gap is normal — it's the client running their own QC — and planning around it is part of the job. What gets taught in the money session later is how that review behaves client by client; what matters today is simply where payment sits on the map: after review, never before it.

How the last mile runs, step by step

  1. The file sits in the client's portal, under review.
  2. Questions, if any, come back — each one is answered with proof, not argument.
  3. The invoice is approved in full, approved in part, or disputed line by line.
  4. Payment arrives for what was approved.
  5. Anything unpaid or unanswered is not closed — it moves, visibly, into follow-up.

If you've done this work before

Here's the discipline worth passing on: a reduced line is information before it's an insult. Reductions cluster — by work type, by proof habit, by crew — and the person doing follow-up is the first to see the pattern. Offices that read their reductions learn; offices that just resent them repeat them. This stop is quietly where the next season's training comes from.

The line to remember: “Done and proven is the middle of the story. Paid is near the end.”

Where this comes from

Payment's place on the map — “comes after the client's review” — is the course materials' own ordering. Timelines and terms differ by client and are taught, where they're taught at all, from each client's own documents in the money session; this page deliberately carries no payment-timing figures.

If this is all new to you

Follow-up is the office's memory, working on purpose. Every submitted order has an expected ending: paid in full, or a explained difference. Follow-up is the habit of comparing the expected ending with the real one — order by order — and chasing the gap while the trail is still warm: the unanswered question in the portal, the line reduced without a reason, the payment that never arrived. An order is only truly finished when someone can account for every dollar it billed and every question it raised.

How follow-up closes an order, step by step

  1. List what's still open: unpaid lines, unanswered questions, unexplained reductions.
  2. Ask, with the proof attached — most answers are already in the file; point at them.
  3. Record every answer against the order, so the next person doesn't re-ask it.
  4. Escalate what won't close — a stuck order handed up beats a stuck order forgotten.
  5. Close the order only when the dollars and the answers both balance.

If you've done this work before

Follow-up is where “pass it on clean, or stop it honestly” gets its final meaning: the last hand on the order doesn't pass it on at all — it accounts for it. Teach trainees to love the closed loop. An office where every order reaches an accounted ending can prove its whole history to anyone, client or auditor, from its own records. That's not admin. That's the company's memory of itself.

The line to remember: “Finished means every dollar and every answer, accounted for.”

Where this comes from

Follow-up's definition is quoted from the course materials: tracking the order “until every dollar and every answer is accounted for.” The chasing discipline above is that definition at work; the detailed collections craft is a later session's subject and isn't pre-taught here.

Chapter 11 · The decision

A cold fridge. A lit clock. Medicine four days old.

A practice case, made up for this classroom. The order says: Secure plus Grass Cut — change the locks and board the broken entries, and cut the overgrown lawn. It sounds simple. Then the crew reports what they found: the fridge is cold. The clock is lit. A prescription is four days old. In pairs: approve, hold, or reject — then write your Update Line.

None of these signs proves someone lives here. Together, they make it impossible to say the house is empty.

Pairs decide — then defend it in writing

Tap your pair's decision to hear how a strong processor reasons it through. Predictions are never graded — reasoning is what's praised, especially reasoned wrong answers, because a trainee who shows their thinking can be taught.

Now write the Update Line

An Update Line tells the next person everything they need — what you saw, what you decided, what happens next — in 25 words or fewer. Type yours and watch the checks.

0 / 25 wordsSignal, decision, next step. Twenty-five words is the whole budget.
  • 25 words or fewer
  • The decision is stated — hold, approve, or reject, in plain words
  • Read yours back: is the occupancy signal named — the thing you actually saw?
  • Read yours back: is the next step named — who does what next?

The strong example, at exactly 20 words: “House may be occupied — fridge cold, clock lit, prescription 4 days old. HOLD. Escalate occupancy check before any secure work.” And the weak one, to never send: “Not sure, maybe wait and see.” No signal, no decision, no next step — it says nothing, and in this job, saying nothing is how mistakes happen.

Say it in class

“A cold fridge. A lit clock. Medicine four days old. Three small signs. One big question: is someone still living here? The answer is HOLD. Escalate the occupancy check before any secure work. We do not know she is empty. We do not know she is lived in. So we do not touch her locks.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

Read the signs the way the crew found them. A cold fridge means food is still being kept cold — someone is keeping this house running. A lit clock means the power is on and the clock is running — the house is not cut off and abandoned. A prescription four days old means medicine was picked up four days ago — someone was out in the world, alive and active, very recently. Now the discipline: none of these proves someone lives here. But proof was never the standard at the gate. The gate asks whether we can honestly say the house is empty — and with these three signs, nobody can.

How to run the lab, step by step

  1. Read the order aloud: Secure plus Grass Cut. Let it sound simple.
  2. Reveal the three signs one at a time, pausing after each. Watch the room change its mind.
  3. Pairs decide — approve, hold, or reject — and commit before any discussion.
  4. Each pair writes its Update Line, 25 words or fewer, all four checks.
  5. Reveal the expert answer last: HOLD and escalate — and praise the reasoning in the wrong answers out loud.

If you've done this work before

Notice what the case is really training: sign-reading under uncertainty. Real houses rarely announce themselves. They whisper — power on, food cold, mail recent, a car that moves. This case gives trainees three clean whispers so they learn the grammar; the field will give them messier ones. And notice the grass in the order: the lawn still needs cutting eventually. HOLD is about the secure, the locks, the entries — the escalation decides what may proceed and what must wait, which is a finer judgement than a flat no.

The line to remember: “Uncertainty is not a reason to guess. Uncertainty is the reason to stop.”

Where this comes from

The case is the course's own practice case, labelled in its materials as a made-up classroom example — fridge, clock, and prescription exactly as taught there, with the expert answer HOLD and escalate. It describes no real house, order, or client.

4 daysThe age of the prescription — the most recent sign of a living person
3 signsCold fridge, lit clock, fresh medicine — none proves, together they prevent “empty”
1 answerHOLD and escalate — the decision the gate was built for

If this is all new to you

An Update Line is a short written message — 25 words or fewer — that tells the next person everything they need: what you saw, what you decided, and what happens next. It passes only if all four checks pass: (1) the occupancy signal is named — the thing you actually saw; (2) the decision is stated — hold, approve, or reject, in plain words; (3) the next step is named — who does what next; (4) it's inside 25 words. The limit isn't style. A short line gets read. A long one gets skimmed, and skimmed lines lose exactly the word that mattered.

How to write one, step by step

  1. Start with the signal: name the strongest thing you saw. “Fridge cold, clock lit.”
  2. State the decision in one plain word, early: HOLD.
  3. Name the next step and its owner: “Escalate occupancy check before any secure work.”
  4. Count the words. Over 25? Cut adjectives, not facts.
  5. Read it as the next person: could they act on this alone, tonight, without calling you? Then send it.

If you've done this work before

The weak example — “Not sure, maybe wait and see” — deserves its moment in class, because everyone in the room has sent some version of it. It fails kindly people, not careless ones: the writer was unsure, honestly. The Update Line's discipline is that honesty isn't enough — the next person needs the signal, the decision, and the step, or your honesty just hands them your uncertainty with nothing to hold it by. Teach the form as a kindness to the night shift.

The line to remember: “Just the signal, the decision, and the next step. No rambling. No guessing.”

Where this comes from

The Update Line, its 25-word budget, and its four checks are the course's own tool, taught in its materials with the strong example (20 words) and the weak one used on this slide — both quoted as the course gives them. The checker on this slide counts words and spots the decision word for you; the signal and next-step checks stay human, because only a reader can judge whether the right signal was named.

Chapter 12 · The close

The work is done and proven. Who pays, how much, and when?

That's where this class leaves the order — built, travelled, proven, submitted, and tracked. What the class keeps isn't the eleven stops; it's the one order they held with their own hands, on a cold fridge and a lit clock. The first order you hold yourself is the one you never forget.

Next class, the toolbox opens: the work itself — grass, and secure — stop five, in your hands at last. But she stays held until the check comes back. Some questions outrank the schedule.

Say it in class

“One order, eleven stops, many hands — and the bravest stop on the wall is the one where somebody said: hold. Hold them well. That is the whole skill.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

On the surface, today taught a route: eleven stops an order travels. Underneath, it taught a temperament. Every stop asked the same question in different clothes — do I actually know this, or am I assuming it? Intake asks it of the order. The gate asks it of the house. QC asks it of the proof. Follow-up asks it of the money. A processor with that temperament can be taught any client, any rulebook, any system. A processor without it is a risk at every stop, however fast their hands are.

How to close the class, step by step

  1. Cover the wall map and have the class say the eleven stops from memory — ragged is fine, complete is the goal.
  2. Ask the only review question that matters: “Where does an unclear right get stopped?” — “At the gate, with a hold.”
  3. Send them out on the held order, not the map: the cold fridge is what they'll remember in the field, and that's exactly right.

If you've done this work before

The course is honest about its own memory anchor: trainees will forget stops and remember the fridge. That's not a failure of the map — it's how people actually carry training into the field, as one vivid case with a rule attached. When you supervise these trainees later, you won't need to re-teach the gate. You'll just need to say “cold fridge” — and watch the whole lesson stand back up.

The line to remember: “The gate is the lesson. The fridge is how they'll remember it.”

Where this comes from

The course materials name this session's memory anchor openly: the first order the trainees held themselves. The retrieval close above is the session's own — rule card and three photos at the open, the held order at the close.

If this is all new to you

Everything so far has circled one stop without entering it: the field. Next class goes inside it — the two kinds of work a new processor meets first. Grass: how a lawn is read, cut, and proven. Secure: locks, boards, and the gate's discipline at the door itself, where today's HOLD lesson stops being a classroom case and becomes a person's actual morning. The map stays on the wall. Now the class starts living at one stop at a time.

How today's map carries forward, step by step

  1. The work sessions (next two classes) live at stops 5–6: field and proof.
  2. The damage session after them teaches reading any house the way the lab read the fridge.
  3. The money session closes the map: stops 8–11, bidding, invoice, and how the three roles share the work.
  4. Every one of those classes opens by pointing at today's wall map. Nothing new floats free of it.

If you've done this work before

One promise to make before the class leaves: the money question hanging over this close — who pays, how much, and when — is not a tease. It's the map's last four stops, and it gets its own full session, with the ladders and the roles, once the work itself is understood. Trainees who know payment is coming as a subject stop inventing answers to it in the meantime.

The line to remember: “The work is done and proven. Who pays, how much, and when — that's a class of its own, and it's coming.”

Where this comes from

The cliffhanger question is the course's own, word for word, and the forward path — work sessions, damage, then money — follows the programme's session order. Nothing about the coming classes' content is pre-taught here beyond their place on the map.

Tip: use the ← and → keys to move between chapters — and open the full notes on any slide to re-learn the topic from scratch

All 12 slides

The full arc of Class 5 on one screen — the rule card recalled, one order's eleven stops, the gate, the hold, and the decision lab. Tap any slide to jump to it.

The logic behind this page

Why Class 5 follows one order instead of teaching eleven topics, why the gate gets three chapters, and what this page does — and doesn't — claim. One teacher to another, before the class walks in.

One order, not eleven lectures

The lifecycle could be taught as eleven definitions in a row, and forgotten by lunch. Instead this page makes one work order the main character and walks it down the wall map, so each stop is learned as something that happens to the order the class is already following. The sequence is the programme's own spine: every later session is a closer look at a stop named here, which is why this page spends its length on the map as a whole rather than drilling any single stop.

Why the gate gets three chapters

  • The gate is the only stop whose failure can't be repaired downstream. A missed scope line can be re-worked; a gap in proof can be re-shot. An unauthorised entry is done the moment it happens. The page weights its chapters by irreversibility, not by how often each stop occurs.
  • HOLD is taught as a decision, not an absence of one. Slide 6 exists so trainees hear, before they ever feel deadline pressure, that stopping is a skilled, praiseworthy act with its own second half — escalation. Offices get the behaviour they honour; this page honours the hold in front of witnesses.
  • The decision lab is never cut. The cold-fridge case is the session's centre: pairs must commit, write, and defend before the reveal. Predictions are never graded, because a graded guess teaches trainees to hide their reasoning — and hidden reasoning is the one thing this course cannot teach past.

Why the Update Line is a machine, not a tip

  • Four checks, all must pass. Signal named, decision stated, next step named, 25 words or fewer. Three out of four is not good enough, because the missing quarter is always the one the next person needed.
  • The checker on Slide 11 automates only what's automatable — the word count and the presence of a plain decision word. Whether the right signal was named is a judgement, so the page leaves it as a read-it-back check rather than pretending software can grade understanding.
  • The strong example is 20 words, counted on the slide, so the class sees the budget is generous for anyone who cuts adjectives instead of facts.

What isn't proven — the open questions, honestly

  • The eleven-stop map is the programme's teaching model of how an order moves through an office like this one. Real companies name and group these stops differently; the map teaches the journey and its dependencies, not any single firm's org chart.
  • The Washington lock-and-possession lesson is taught as the programme's courtroom illustration of why authority comes first. It is not legal advice, and other jurisdictions write their own rules — a real legal question goes to the client's rulebook and up the chain.
  • No rates, fees, or payment timings appear on this page, deliberately: pricing and terms differ by client and belong to the money session, sourced from each client's own documents.
  • The decision-lab case is a made-up classroom example, labelled as such on its slide. It describes no real house, order, client, or crew.
  • Nothing here is real client data — the house is a teaching character carried from Class 1, and every stop is taught from the programme's own course materials.

Running the class from this page

  • Open cold. Slide 1 is a recall before it is a welcome: rule card first, three photos second, five minutes, then move on. Do not re-teach the proof lesson; ask the questions that lead back to it.
  • Build the map once, then keep pointing at it. Every chapter after Slide 3 names its stop number. If a discussion drifts, the question “which stop are we on?” ends the drift.
  • Protect the lab. If time runs short, cut discussion elsewhere — never the pairs' decision and Update Line on Slide 11. The held order is the memory anchor; the map can be re-read, the anchor can't be re-lived.
  • Praise holds by name. In the lab and ever after: when someone calls a hold and defends it, honour it in front of the room. That is how the gate survives contact with real deadlines.
  • This page is the spine, not a guest. If a live Muse segment joins the class, it belongs in the Muse app, projected, in one short mid-class slot — and this page can still carry the whole lesson if the connection ever fails.

Where it all came from

Every teaching point on the slides names its home in its drawer. In short:

  • The whole session — story spine, the eleven stops and their definitions, the permission gate, occupancy, HOLD and escalate, the cold-fridge decision case, the Update Line and its four checks, the strong and weak examples, and the teacher's lines — comes from the programme's own blueprint for Session 5, “The Order: One Work Order, Start to Finish.”
  • The rule card (“Permission first. Proof always.”) and the three photographs (mail, camera, portal) are carried over from the preceding class, as the blueprint directs.
  • The Washington lock-and-possession point is carried as the programme teaches it, flagged on its slide as a teaching illustration rather than legal advice.
  • Plus the earlier classes themselves — the house, her name, the fall, and the system — leaned on here rather than re-proven.

This is the demo version of Class 5 from the preservation training programme — shared so the teacher can look it over before the full class is built. Our house is a teaching character, made up for the story; the pictures are illustrations, not a real property. The work order, the cold-fridge case, and every example on this page are teaching examples — no real clients, work orders, addresses, or company details anywhere on the page.
